title: How people learned about the sky, and made clocks and calendars from it

summary.text: Long before clocks and phones, people in Babylon, Greece, India, China and the Maya lands watched the sky every night and wrote down what they saw. They found that the sky repeats: the Sun gives the day, the Moon gives the month, and the Sun's slow journey gives the year. Every calendar in the world is built from these three repeats. To count time at night, people made water clocks, such as the Indian ghati, a bowl with a hole that sinks in a set time. In this unit you build one, and find out how steady it really is. You also meet Parameshvara, a Kerala astronomer who showed that old tables of the sky had drifted, by watching eclipses for most of his life.
summary.art: A night sky over a flat terrace, with faint pictures around the edge: a Babylonian clay tablet, a Greek stick and shadow, an Indian copper bowl floating in water, a Chinese star map and a Maya stone calendar.

intro.hook: Close your eyes. Say 'now' when you think one minute has passed. A grown-up checks with a clock. Were you early or late? Before clocks, how did people know the time at night?
intro.text: Your own sense of time drifts, so people looked for something steadier. They found it in the sky. The Sun rises again every morning. The Moon grows full about every 29 and a half days. The Sun comes back to the same place among the seasons every 365 days. People counted these repeats and made calendars. They made water clocks to count the hours between sunset and sunrise. In this unit you make a sinking cup clock, test how steady it is, and meet the sky-watchers who taught the world to count time.
intro.art: A child sitting with eyes closed on a sofa, and a mother beside her watching the seconds on a wall clock.

outcomes: I can name the three repeats in the sky that give us the day, the month and the year, and say how long each one takes.
I can explain why a calendar that counts only Moon months drifts away from the seasons.
I can build a sinking cup water clock, time it three times, and say how steady it was, using my own results.
I can say one thing that each of these people found out about the sky: the Babylonians, the Greeks, Indian astronomers, the Chinese and the Maya.
I can tell how Parameshvara of Kerala showed that old tables of the sky had drifted, by watching eclipses.
I can explain why people checked their clocks and calendars against the sky for thousands of years.
I can find the sky in our own calendar: in nazhigai, in month names, and in festivals that follow the Sun or the Moon.

terms.meaning: The study of the Sun, Moon, stars, planets and everything else in the sky.
terms.example: Watching the Moon each night and drawing its shape is a small piece of astronomy.
terms.art: A girl on a balcony drawing the Moon in a notebook.

terms.meaning: A person who studies the sky. Long ago, astronomers watched with their eyes and wrote down what they saw.
terms.example: Aryabhata was an astronomer in India about 1,500 years ago.
terms.art: An old astronomer sitting on a roof at night, pointing at a star and writing on a palm leaf.

terms.meaning: A way of counting days, months and years, so people can plan ahead and agree on dates.
terms.example: The calendar on your kitchen wall shows Pournami, Amavasya and festival days.
terms.art: A wall calendar in a kitchen with small Moon shapes printed on some dates.

terms.meaning: The time from one full Moon to the next, about 29 and a half days. 'Lunar' means to do with the Moon.
terms.example: From one Pournami to the next is one lunar month.
terms.art: A row of Moon shapes from full to thin to full again, with '29 and a half days' written under them.

terms.meaning: The time the Earth takes to go once round the Sun, about 365 and a quarter days. It brings the seasons back. 'Solar' means to do with the Sun.
terms.example: Pongal comes in the middle of January every year, because it follows the Sun.
terms.art: The Earth on a circle round the Sun, with mango trees in four seasons drawn around the circle.

terms.meaning: One of 27 star groups along the Moon's path in Indian astronomy. The Moon moves into a new one about every day.
terms.example: Onam falls when the Moon is in the nakshatra Thiruvonam.
terms.art: A curved band of stars with 27 small star groups, and the Moon sitting in one of them.

terms.meaning: An old Indian unit of time, 24 minutes long. There are 60 nazhigai in one day and night. In Sanskrit it is called a ghatika or ghati.
terms.example: A Tamil panchangam still gives some times in nazhigai.
terms.art: A clock face split into 60 small parts, with one part shaded and labelled 24 minutes.

terms.meaning: A clock that measures time by water flowing in or out of a bowl at a steady rate.
terms.example: The Indian ghati was a copper bowl with a tiny hole. Floating in water, it filled and sank in one nazhigai.
terms.art: A copper bowl floating in a big pot of water, half full, with a tiny stream of water coming in through its hole.

terms.meaning: A clock that tells the time from the shadow of a stick or a wall in sunlight.
terms.example: The huge sundial at Jantar Mantar in Jaipur casts a shadow that moves across a curved scale.
terms.art: A stick standing in sunlight on a flat stone, with its shadow pointing to a marked line.

terms.meaning: When one sky body blocks the light of another. In a lunar eclipse, the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.
terms.example: Old astronomers could say in advance on which night a lunar eclipse would happen.
terms.art: A full Moon with a curved dark shadow covering part of it.

terms.meaning: A written note of what you saw and when, kept so you or others can look back at it.
terms.example: Babylonian sky-watchers wrote nightly records on clay tablets for hundreds of years.
terms.art: A clay tablet covered in small wedge-shaped marks, next to a child's notebook with dates and drawings.

terms.meaning: Something that happens again and again in the same order, taking the same time.
terms.example: Full Moon, half Moon, no Moon, half Moon, full Moon again is a cycle.
terms.art: A circle of arrows with the Moon's shapes around it.

terms.meaning: A careful guess about what will happen, made from what you already know.
terms.example: Knowing the Moon's cycle, you can predict the date of the next Pournami.
terms.art: A girl pointing at a future date on a calendar where she has drawn a full Moon.

terms.meaning: A place built for watching the sky and measuring it.
terms.example: Jantar Mantar in Jaipur and Delhi are observatories built of stone, nearly 300 years ago.
terms.art: Large stone instruments with staircases and curved scales at Jantar Mantar, under a blue sky.

terms.meaning: The day when the Sun rises and sets furthest north or furthest south in the year. It seems to stop there and turn back.
terms.example: Around 21 June, the Sun sets at its furthest point north, so the day is longest in India.
terms.art: A window with tape marks showing where the Sun set on different dates, the marks bunched together at one end.

explanations.definition: The sky has three big repeats. The Earth turns once a day. The Moon goes through its shapes in about 29 and a half days. The Earth goes round the Sun in about 365 and a quarter days.
explanations.description: Every morning the Sun rises in the east, crosses the sky and sets in the west. This happens because the Earth turns once each day. Every night the Moon looks a little different. After about 29 and a half days it comes back to the same shape. Over the year, the Sun rises a little further north or south each day, and the noon shadow grows longer and shorter. After about 365 days it starts again. People everywhere noticed these three repeats. Each one became a unit for counting time: the day, the month and the year.
examples: The word 'month' comes from the same old word as 'Moon'.
In Tamil, 'thingal' can mean both the Moon and a month.
The Sun takes about 365 days to come back to rising at the same point on the horizon.
explanations.art: Three circles side by side: the Earth spinning, the Moon's shapes in a ring, and the Earth going round the Sun.
explanations.context: This card is about the three repeats in the sky that every calendar is built from.

explanations.concept: Calendars from the Sun and from the Moon
explanations.definition: A solar calendar follows the Sun, so it stays with the seasons. A lunar calendar follows the Moon's months. A calendar that uses both adds an extra month now and then to stay in step.
explanations.description: Twelve Moon months add up to about 354 days. That is about 11 days short of the Sun's year. So a calendar of only Moon months slides away from the seasons. The Islamic Hijri calendar is a Moon calendar, so Ramzan comes about 11 days earlier each year. Most Indian Hindu calendars use both. They count Moon months, but add an extra month, the adhika masa, about every two and a half to three years. Then the festivals stay in their seasons. The calendar on most Indian walls today, the Gregorian calendar, follows only the Sun. It adds a leap day on 29 February in most fourth years.
examples: Pongal follows the Sun, so it falls in the middle of January every year.
Deepavali follows the Moon, so its date moves between October and November.
Onam needs both: the Sun's month of Chingam and the Moon in the nakshatra Thiruvonam.
explanations.art: Two wheels side by side, one with a Sun in the middle and 12 seasons, one with a Moon in the middle and 12 Moon shapes, with a small extra slice added to the Moon wheel.
explanations.context: This card is about the two kinds of calendar, and why Moon months need an extra month added now and then.

explanations.definition: Before clocks with gears, people used shadows to tell the time by day, and water flowing through a small hole to measure time at night.
explanations.description: A stick in the sun casts a shadow that moves as the Earth turns. That is a sundial. But a sundial is no use at night or on a cloudy day. So people made water clocks. In Babylon, Egypt and China, water dripped out of one pot into another, and marks showed the time. In India, astronomers used the ghati, also called the ghatika. It was a copper bowl with a tiny hole in the bottom. It floated in a big pot of water, slowly filled, and sank. Then someone emptied it and floated it again. The old Indian astronomy book called the Surya Siddhanta describes such a bowl. The bowl was made so that it sank 60 times in one day and night, once every 24 minutes. The Tamil word for this time is nazhigai, and the Hindi word for a clock, ghadi, comes from ghati.
examples: The Tamil unit nazhigai is 24 minutes, one sixtieth of a day.
An old water pot found at Karnak in Egypt, more than 3,000 years old, has marks inside for the hours.
In China, an official named Su Song built a tall water-powered clock tower that also turned a model of the sky, around the year 1090.
explanations.art: A copper bowl floating in a large brass pot of water, beside a sundial stick on a stone, under a half-day, half-night sky.
explanations.context: This card is about how people told the time before clocks with gears: sundials by day and water clocks by night.

explanations.concept: The Babylonians: writing the sky down
explanations.definition: The Babylonians lived in what is now Iraq. They wrote down what they saw in the sky night after night on clay tablets, and found patterns that let them predict eclipses.
explanations.description: The Babylonians wrote by pressing a reed into wet clay. For hundreds of years, their sky-watchers kept records of the Moon, the planets and the weather. Many of these tablets still survive. Because they kept records for so long, they found repeats too slow to notice in one lifetime. Eclipses of the Moon follow a pattern that repeats about every 18 years, and the Babylonians used it to say in advance when one might happen. They counted in sixties. That is why we still have 60 seconds in a minute, 60 minutes in an hour and 360 degrees in a circle.
examples: Babylonian records of the planet Venus rising and setting were written on clay more than 2,500 years ago.
Thousands of Babylonian sky tablets are kept in the British Museum in London.
Every time you read a clock, you count minutes the Babylonian way, in sixties.
explanations.art: A woman pressing a reed into a wet clay tablet by lamplight, with the Moon and a bright planet outside a doorway.
explanations.context: This card is about the Babylonians, who kept written records of the sky for centuries.

explanations.concept: The Greeks: asking why, and measuring the Earth
explanations.definition: Greek thinkers tried to explain why the sky moves as it does, and used shadows and angles to measure the size of the Earth.
explanations.description: Around 240 BCE, Eratosthenes worked in the great library of Alexandria in Egypt. He learned that at noon on one day of the year, the Sun shone straight down a well in the town of Syene, further south. On the same day in Alexandria, a stick cast a short shadow. From the angle of that shadow and the distance between the towns, he worked out the size of the whole Earth, and got close to the real size. Hipparchus made a list of about 850 stars and found that the stars slowly shift over centuries. Most Greeks thought the Earth stood still in the middle of everything, with the Sun and planets on perfect circles. Hypatia, a woman astronomer and teacher in Alexandria, worked on the great astronomy book by Ptolemy about 1,600 years ago.
examples: Eratosthenes measured the Earth with a shadow, a distance and some careful thinking, without leaving Egypt.
Aristarchus, a Greek, said the Earth goes round the Sun, but almost nobody agreed with him for nearly 1,800 years.
Hypatia taught astronomy and mathematics in Alexandria until she was killed in the year 415.
explanations.art: A stick casting a short shadow in Alexandria and a well with sunlight going straight down in Syene, with a curved Earth drawn between them.
explanations.context: This card is about the Greek sky-watchers, who asked why the sky moves and measured the Earth with a shadow.

explanations.concept: India: Jyotisha, nakshatras and the Kerala astronomers
explanations.definition: Jyotisha is the old Indian study of the sky and of time. Indian astronomers divided the Moon's path into 27 nakshatras, worked out calendars, and calculated eclipses.
explanations.description: The oldest Indian book about the sky is the Vedanga Jyotisha. It is more than 2,000 years old, though its exact age is argued about. It sets out a calendar for rituals, using the Sun, the Moon and the nakshatras. The Moon takes about 27 days to go round the sky past the same stars, so it spends about one day in each nakshatra. Many month names come from the nakshatra where the full Moon sits. Chaitra comes from Chitra, and Karthigai from Krittika. In 499, Aryabhata wrote that the Earth spins, and that eclipses are shadows. Much later, astronomers in Kerala, such as Madhava, Parameshvara and Nilakantha, did new mathematics and checked their numbers against the sky. Around 1730, Raja Jai Singh II built huge stone observatories, the Jantar Mantars, in Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Varanasi and Mathura.
examples: The Tamil month Karthigai is named after Krittika, the star group also called the Pleiades.
Karthigai Deepam is lit on the full Moon when the Moon is in Krittika.
The Jantar Mantar in Jaipur has a sundial as tall as a nine-storey building.
explanations.art: A palm-leaf manuscript with star diagrams beside an oil lamp, and behind it the outline of the Jaipur Jantar Mantar under stars.
explanations.context: This card is about sky-watching in India: the nakshatras, Aryabhata, the Kerala astronomers and Jantar Mantar.

explanations.concept: China: the longest records of the sky
explanations.definition: Chinese astronomers kept careful written records of the sky for over 2,000 years, including comets, eclipses and new stars.
explanations.description: In China, astronomers worked for the emperor. Their job was to watch the sky every night and write down anything new. They noted comets, sunspots and eclipses. In the year 1054, they wrote about a 'guest star' that suddenly appeared, so bright it could be seen in the daytime for weeks. Today we know it was an exploding star. Its cloud of leftover gas, the Crab Nebula, is still there, and it is still spreading out. Chinese astronomers also divided the sky along the Moon's path into 28 parts, called lodges, a little like the Indian nakshatras.
examples: Chinese records of Halley's Comet go back to 240 BCE.
Astronomers today still use the Chinese record of 1054 to work out how old the Crab Nebula is.
Wang Zhenyi, a young woman in China in the 1700s, wrote books on astronomy and explained how eclipses happen.
explanations.art: A Chinese astronomer at night on a tiled roof, brush in hand, looking up at an unusually bright new star.
explanations.context: This card is about Chinese astronomers, who kept records of the sky for over 2,000 years.

explanations.definition: The Maya lived in what is now Mexico and Central America. They tracked the planet Venus and built calendars that fit several sky cycles together.
explanations.description: The Maya watched Venus very closely. Venus appears as a bright morning star, disappears, then appears as an evening star, and comes back to the morning about every 584 days. A Maya book called the Dresden Codex has a table of Venus's appearances, worked out far into the future. Five Venus cycles are 2,920 days, which is exactly eight years of 365 days. The Maya also used a 365-day year and a 260-day count. The two counts line up again every 52 years.
examples: 5 times 584 is 2,920, and 8 times 365 is also 2,920.
The Dresden Codex is a folded Maya book about 800 years old, now kept in Dresden in Germany.
At the pyramid of El Castillo in Mexico, around 21 March and 22 September, the late afternoon Sun casts a shadow on the staircase that looks like a snake.
explanations.art: A painted Maya book page with dots and bars for numbers, and a bright Venus low over a stone pyramid at dawn.
explanations.context: This card is about the Maya, who counted the cycles of the planet Venus.

explanations.concept: Why people checked their clocks and calendars against the sky
explanations.definition: A water clock or a calculated table drifts a little from the truth over time. The sky's repeats are much steadier, so people corrected their clocks and calendars by watching the sky.
explanations.description: A ghati bowl sinks a little faster or slower if the water is warmer, if the hole wears or if it is put down roughly. So astronomers checked it against the Sun and stars. Calculated tables of the sky drift too. Small errors in the numbers add up over hundreds of years. Parameshvara, in Kerala, saw that eclipses were not happening at the times the old tables said. He watched eclipses for decades and wrote a new, corrected system in 1431. Even the second was measured from the Earth's movement until 1967. Since then, it is measured with atomic clocks, which are steadier still.
examples: The sinking cup in this unit sinks in a slightly different time each round.
Old tables made in 683 had drifted from the sky by the 1400s, and Parameshvara corrected them.
Since 1972, a leap second has sometimes been added to clocks, because the Earth's spin is not perfectly steady.
explanations.art: A copper water bowl next to a night sky with the Moon partly in shadow, and an astronomer comparing a palm-leaf table with the eclipse.
explanations.context: This card explains why clocks and calendars were always corrected by watching the sky.

explanations.concept: Why do we count minutes in sixties?
explanations.description: We know that the Babylonians counted in sixties, and that we got 60 minutes and 360 degrees from their astronomy. Why they chose 60 is not known for sure. There are a few ideas.
examples: 60 can be split evenly into 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30 parts.
You can count 12 finger joints on one hand with your thumb, and 5 fingers on the other hand make 5 lots of 12, which is 60.

perspectives.explanation: 60 splits evenly in many ways, so it is easy to share things into halves, thirds, quarters and fifths without fractions.
Two older counting systems, one in tens and one in sixes or twelves, may have been joined together.
People may have counted 12 finger joints on one hand with the thumb, and kept track of 5 lots of 12 on the other hand.

explanations.art: A child's two hands, the right thumb touching the joints of the right fingers, and the left hand holding up fingers to keep count.
explanations.context: This card is about why we count 60 minutes in an hour. Nobody knows for sure, so here are the main ideas.

explanations.concept: Did sky-watchers learn from each other?
explanations.description: Some ideas clearly travelled. Greek astronomy reached India about 1,800 years ago, and Indian books from that time use some Greek words. Later, Indian numbers and astronomy reached Baghdad, and from there Europe. For older times, historians argue.
examples: The Sanskrit word 'hora', for an hour, is thought to come from Greek.
Indian books on astronomy were translated into Arabic in Baghdad in the 700s.

perspectives.explanation: The Vedanga Jyotisha calendar has numbers similar to Babylonian ones, so they think Babylonian ideas reached India early.
The Vedanga Jyotisha grew out of Indian ritual needs, and anyone watching the same sky would find similar numbers. So the likeness does not prove copying.
The Maya had no contact with Asia or Europe, and still found the same Moon month and year, because they watched the same sky.

explanations.art: A map with arrows between Babylon, Greece, India, China and Baghdad, and the Maya lands far away across the ocean with no arrow.
explanations.context: This card is about whether sky-watchers in different lands learned from each other. Historians argue, and here are the sides.

agreed.text: The day comes from the Earth turning, the month from the Moon's cycle, and the year from the Earth going round the Sun.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can watch the Sun rise each day, the Moon change over a month, and the noon shadow change through the year.

agreed.text: Twelve Moon months are about 11 days shorter than a solar year.
agreed.evidence: Twelve times 29 and a half is 354 days, and a solar year is about 365 days. Ramzan moves about 11 days earlier each year in the Gregorian calendar.

agreed.text: Babylonian astronomers kept written records of the sky for centuries, and we still count 60 minutes in an hour and 360 degrees in a circle because of them.
agreed.evidence: Thousands of their clay tablets survive and have been read by historians.

agreed.text: Chinese astronomers recorded a new star in 1054, and it was an exploding star whose remains are the Crab Nebula.
agreed.evidence: The Crab Nebula is spreading out. Working backwards from its speed gives a start date close to 1054.

agreed.text: Indian astronomers used sinking bowl water clocks that measured one ghatika, 24 minutes.
agreed.evidence: They are described in Indian astronomy books such as the Surya Siddhanta, and the unit survives in Tamil as nazhigai.

challenging.claim: Ancient people did not know the Earth is round.
challenging.for: Many old pictures show a flat world, and people often say that sailors feared falling off the edge.
challenging.against: Greek thinkers knew the Earth is round by about 350 BCE, from the curved shadow of the Earth on the Moon during eclipses. Eratosthenes measured its size. Aryabhata in India also wrote that the Earth is a sphere.
challenging.context: This card is about a common mistake: that people long ago all thought the Earth was flat.

challenging.claim: The Earth stands still in the middle, and the Sun, Moon and stars go round it.
challenging.who: Most Greek astronomers, including Ptolemy, and most of the world for about 1,800 years
challenging.for: The ground feels still, and the Sun really does seem to go round us every day.
challenging.against: Aryabhata said the Earth spins. Copernicus and Galileo showed that the Earth goes round the Sun. Today spacecraft see it.
challenging.context: This card is about the old idea that the Earth stands still at the centre of everything.

challenging.claim: The heavens are perfect and never change.
challenging.for: The stars keep the same patterns year after year, so the sky seems fixed for ever.
challenging.against: Chinese astronomers recorded a 'guest star' in 1054 that appeared and faded. Comets come and go. The stars also shift slowly over centuries, as Hipparchus found.
challenging.context: This card is about the old idea that nothing in the sky ever changes.

challenging.claim: The Maya calendar said the world would end in 2012.
challenging.who: Many films, websites and newspapers around 2012
challenging.for: One long Maya count of days reached a round number in December 2012.
challenging.against: Maya experts say it was like a car's meter rolling over to a new round number. Maya writings mention dates long after 2012. Nothing happened.
challenging.context: This card is about a popular story that the Maya predicted the end of the world.

challenging.claim: The positions of the planets when you are born decide what kind of person you will be.
challenging.who: Astrology, in many cultures. In India, the old Jyotisha books included both astronomy and astrology.
challenging.for: Astrology is very old, many families use it, and people often feel their reading fits them.
challenging.against: When scientists tested it, astrologers could not match birth charts to people's characters better than by chance. One such test was published in the journal Nature in 1985. Astronomy, the study of where things are and how they move, works very well.
challenging.context: This card is about astrology, the idea that the sky shapes our lives, and what tests have found.

challenging.claim: Water clocks were too rough to be useful.
challenging.for: A bowl with a hole can be put down roughly, the hole can wear, and the water temperature changes.
challenging.against: Astronomers checked them against the stars, and made them carefully. Water clocks were used for over 2,000 years in Egypt, Babylon, Greece, China, India and the Arab world. Your own cup clock may be steady to within a few seconds.
challenging.context: This card is about whether old water clocks were any good.

big_questions.q: Your sense of a minute drifted, and your cup clock drifted a little too. Is there any clock that does not drift at all?
big_questions.hint: Think about the cup, the Moon, the turning Earth and the atomic clocks that set your phone.

big_questions.q: If you lived in a cave with no clocks and no sky, how would you know how many days had passed?
big_questions.hint: Think about sleep, hunger and your heartbeat. People who have tried this lost count.

big_questions.q: The Maya and the Babylonians never met, yet both counted a month of about 29 and a half days. What does that tell us about the sky?
big_questions.hint: Two people measuring the same thing carefully get the same answer.

big_questions.q: Is time something that exists out there, or is it only our way of counting the sky's repeats?
big_questions.hint: Would time still pass if nothing in the universe repeated?

big_questions.q: A plant flowers when the nights grow long enough. Does a plant have a calendar?
big_questions.hint: Many plants measure the length of the night. What else in nature keeps count of the seasons?

big_questions.q: Parameshvara spent 55 years watching eclipses to correct one table. Is that a good way to spend a life?
big_questions.hint: Think about who used his tables after him, and what it is like to find something out for certain.

story.title: Paati's Night Clock
story.note: The story is made up. The facts in it are true: a nazhigai is 24 minutes, the old Indian ghati bowl sank once each nazhigai, and the Moon moves across the sky by about one fist held at arm's length every 40 minutes.
text: It was a Sunday night in Madurai, and Sunday nights in Meenakshi's family had one rule. No phones, no TV, no screens of any kind. All the phones went into a steel box on top of the fridge at six o'clock.
Meenakshi was nine. Her brother Karthik was six. Amma had gone to Chennai for work, and her train would reach Madurai at nine o'clock. Appa was going to the station on his scooter to fetch her.
"How long till nine?" asked Karthik, for the fourth time.
Just before Appa went out to buy milk, he had said, "It is half past seven." Now he was gone. The wall clock in the hall had stopped, because its cell was flat. And the phones were in the box.
"We could open the box," said Karthik.

"Rule is rule," said Paati, their grandmother. She was sitting on the swing on the balcony, looking at the sky. "When I was small, in our village, there was no clock in our house at all. Do you know how my own paati knew the time?"
Karthik shook his head.

"By day, she looked at shadows. At night, she looked up." Paati pointed. The Moon was rising over the temple towers, big and nearly full. "The sky turns all night, slowly and steadily. Watch the Moon, and you can tell how much time has gone by."
"But how much is a lot of Moon?" asked Karthik.

Paati held her fist out at the end of her straight arm. "The Moon moves about this far, one fist, in a little less than an hour. About 40 minutes." She closed one eye. "Right now, the Moon is one fist above the top of the east tower."
"That is too slow to watch," said Karthik. "I want to count."

Meenakshi had an idea. She had read about it in her science book. "In the old days, astronomers had a clock made of water. A copper bowl with a tiny hole. It floats in a big pot, fills up slowly and sinks. Then you empty it and float it again."
"The ghati," said Paati, smiling. "In Tamil we called that time a nazhigai. Twenty-four minutes. Sixty of them in a day and a night."

Meenakshi ran to the kitchen. She found a small plastic cup, the kind left over from a birthday party. Paati heated a needle over the gas flame and made a small hole in the bottom. Meenakshi taped two one-rupee coins inside, so it would sink when full. Karthik dragged in the big steel vessel they used for soaking rice, and filled it with water.
Meenakshi set the cup gently on the water. It bobbed and floated. Then, very slowly, water started to come up through the hole, like a tiny spring.
They waited. The cup sat lower and lower. Then, with a soft gulp, it tipped and went under.
"One!" shouted Karthik.
Meenakshi fished the cup out, poured the water away and floated it again. Karthik made a mark on a paper for each sinking. Two. Three. Four. Five.
"Now we know how long one sinking is," said Karthik proudly.
"Do we?" asked Paati. "What does one sinking mean? Is it one minute? Ten minutes?"
Karthik frowned. The cup could count. But it could not tell him what it was counting.
Meenakshi looked up. She held out her fist at the end of her arm, the way Paati had. The Moon was now about one fist higher than before, two fists above the tower.
"The Moon has moved one fist," she said slowly. "That is about 40 minutes. And the cup sank five times. So one sinking is about 8 minutes."
Paati clapped her hands. "Now your clock has a meaning. The cup counts. The sky tells you what the count is worth."
"So how long till nine?" asked Karthik.

They worked it out together. Appa had said half past seven just when Paati first looked at the Moon. Forty minutes later made it about ten past eight. That left about 50 minutes till nine, which was about six more sinkings.
Karthik counted every one. The cup filled, tipped and sank. Meenakshi emptied it each time. On the sixth sinking, Karthik shouted, "Nine o'clock!"
Just then Appa came up the stairs with the milk. He had stopped to talk to a neighbour on the way. "What time is it?" both children shouted. Appa looked at his watch. "Six minutes past nine. Why?"
"We were only six minutes off!" said Meenakshi. "And we used a cup and the Moon." Appa laughed, picked up his keys and hurried off to the station.
"The cup was not quite the same each time," Meenakshi told Paati. "Once I put it down hard, and it sank faster."
"That is why the old astronomers checked their water clocks against the sky," said Paati. "The cup can be bumped. The Moon cannot."
When Amma came home, Karthik was already asleep on the swing, with five marks, and then six more, on his paper.
story.epiphany: For the parent: a water clock counts steadily, but on its own it does not say how long each count is. Meenakshi gave her cup a meaning by comparing it with the sky. The Moon moved one fist, about 40 minutes, while the cup sank five times, so each sinking was about 8 minutes. Old astronomers did the same with the ghati bowl. They made it sink in one nazhigai, and kept checking it against the Sun and stars, because a bowl can drift and the sky drifts far less.
ask: Why could the cup count, but not tell Karthik the time on its own?
How did Meenakshi work out how long one sinking took?
Why did the cup sink faster when Meenakshi put it down hard?
Paati said the cup can be bumped but the Moon cannot. What did she mean?
How could you use your fist and the Moon to tell how long a film lasts?

experiments.title: The Sinking Cup Clock: does it sink in the same time every round?
experiments.question: Indian astronomers used a bowl with a hole that sank in a set time. If you float the same cup again and again, does it sink in exactly the same time each round?
experiments.predict: Will the cup take exactly the same time each round, nearly the same, or very different times? Why do you think so? Then guess: if the hole is made a little bigger, will the cup sink faster or slower, and why?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same cup, the same hole, the same vessel and the same water for rounds 1, 2 and 3. Lower the cup gently, flat on the water, each time. Start the timer the moment the cup touches the water, and stop it the moment the rim goes under. Empty and shake the cup dry before each round. Only in round 4 do you change one thing, the size of the hole.

materials.item: a light plastic cup, about 150 to 200 ml, such as a disposable cup or a clean curd cup with straight sides. Not a paper cup, which goes soft.
two coins of the same kind, such as one-rupee or two-rupee coins, and cello tape
a big steel vessel, patila or bucket, with water at least 12 cm deep, wider than the cup by a hand on each side
a drawing pin or a thick sewing needle, and a ballpoint pen refill to widen the hole
a phone stopwatch, or a clock with a seconds hand
a notebook and pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up makes the hole, because pins and needles are sharp. Do it on a wooden board, pushing away from the hand. Wipe up spilt water at once so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Make a sinking cup clock. Time it three times, then once with a bigger hole. Compare the times.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then circle the shortest and the longest time from rounds 1 to 3, and write how many seconds apart they are.

flow.do: 1. Tape the two coins flat in the centre of the cup's bottom, inside. 2. Push the pin through the middle of the bottom, between the coins if there is a gap, or next to them. 3. Twist the pen refill tip in the hole to widen it to about 2 millimetres, the width of the refill's tip.
flow.say: Long ago in India, astronomers used a copper bowl with a tiny hole, called a ghati. It floated, slowly filled, and sank. We are making our own. The coins make sure it sinks when it is full.
flow.kid: We are making a water clock. It is a cup with a tiny hole. The coins help it sink.
flow.parent: The hole size decides the time. A hole about 2 millimetres across in a 200 ml cup usually takes about 2 to 8 minutes. You will test this in the next step and adjust if needed.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sinking Cup Clock. Here you make the cup: coins inside, and a small hole in the bottom.

flow.do: 1. Fill the vessel with water at least 12 cm deep. 2. Lower the cup gently, flat on the water. 3. Start the stopwatch. 4. Watch until the rim goes under, and stop the stopwatch.
flow.say: Let's try it once, just to see. Watch the bottom of the cup. Can you see water coming in? Tell me when the rim goes under.
flow.kid: Put the cup gently on the water. Start the timer. Watch the water come in. Stop the timer when it sinks.
flow.parent: This is a practice round. If the cup takes more than 8 minutes, widen the hole a little and try again. If it sinks in under a minute, start again with a new cup and a smaller hole. Once it takes between 2 and 8 minutes, keep this cup. If the cup tips over early, move the coins to the very centre.
flow.context: This is the practice round of the Sinking Cup Clock. You check that your cup takes between 2 and 8 minutes to sink.

flow.do: Ask for a prediction and a reason, and write both down before the timed rounds.
flow.say: Now we will float it three times in exactly the same way. Will it take exactly the same time each round? Nearly the same? Or very different? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Same time every round? Nearly the same? Very different? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the times will be the same, or different?
good: Same, because it is the same cup and the same hole.
A little different, because I might put it down differently.

flow.parent: Do not say what will happen. Any reason your child gives is good. Write down the guess, so you can compare it with the results.

flow.do: 1. Empty the cup, shake out the water and float it gently. 2. Time it until the rim goes under. 3. Write the time. 4. Do rounds 2 and 3 in exactly the same way.
flow.say: Let's do round 1. Put it down as gently as you can. Start the timer the moment it touches the water. Now we wait and watch.
flow.kid: Round 1. Shake the cup dry. Float it gently. Start the timer. Write the time when it sinks. Do it three times.
flow.parent: The times are usually close but not exactly the same, often a few seconds to about half a minute apart. A drop of water left in the cup, a tilt as it goes down, or a bump on the vessel can change the time. Write down anything that happened differently in the last column. If all three times match to the second, that is a real result too. Ask your child what would happen over 60 rounds.
flow.think: If each round can be a few seconds off, how far off could the cup be after 60 rounds, a whole day and night?

flow.do: 1. Ask for a guess: will a bigger hole make it sink faster or slower, and why? 2. Widen the hole by pushing the refill tip in a little further. 3. Time one more round.
flow.say: Now we change just one thing, the hole. If the hole is bigger, will the cup sink faster or slower? Why do you think so? Let's find out.
flow.kid: Now the hole is bigger. Will it sink faster or slower? Why? Try it.
flow.parent: A bigger hole lets water in faster, so the cup sinks sooner. Old clock makers had to get the hole exactly right, so that the bowl sank once every 24 minutes, one nazhigai.

check.q: Round 4 had a bigger hole. What happened?
options: The cup sank sooner, because water came in faster
The cup sank later, because the hole let air out
It made no difference
check.why: A bigger hole lets more water in each second, so the cup fills and sinks sooner. If your cup sank later, check that the hole really got bigger and that the cup went down gently. The hole size is what sets the clock's time, which is why makers of the ghati were careful with it.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think about our cup clock now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think the times were not all exactly the same?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer: what I think, the cup clock is nearly steady but not perfect. What I saw, rounds 1 to 3 took 3 minutes 10, 3 minutes 22 and 3 minutes 5 seconds, so 17 seconds between the shortest and longest. Why, small changes in how I put it down and leftover water changed the time a little. That is why astronomers checked their water clocks against the Sun and stars.

check.q: Your cup sank in slightly different times each round. What did old astronomers do about this in their water clocks?
options: They checked them against the Sun and stars, which repeat more steadily
They used a new cup every round
They did nothing, because a few seconds never matter
check.why: The sky's repeats, the day and the turning stars, are much steadier than any bowl of water. So astronomers set their water clocks by the sky. A new cup every round would make things worse, because each hole is a little different. A few seconds each round add up to minutes over a whole night.

experiments.context: In this experiment you build a sinking cup water clock like the Indian ghati, and test whether it sinks in exactly the same time every round.

experiments.title: The Fist Ruler: does a child's fist measure the same piece of sky as a grown-up's?
experiments.question: Sky-watchers measured how far apart things in the sky were by holding up a fist at arm's length. A child's fist is smaller than a grown-up's. Do they measure the same distance across the sky?
experiments.predict: Stand in one spot and measure the gap between two things on a far wall, in fists. Who will count more fists, you or your grown-up? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both of you stand on the same spot, with one eye closed, and the arm fully straight. Measure the same gap three times each and take the middle answer.

materials.item: two things on a far wall or across the room to measure between, such as the two edges of a door or a window
a measuring tape or a long ruler
a notebook and pencil

experiments.safety: Never measure near the Sun. Do this indoors or at night.

schedule.what: Measure a gap in fists, child and grown-up. Then measure your fists and arms. Compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Write who counted more fists, and whose fist covers a bigger piece of the view.

flow.do: 1. Stand about 4 metres from a wall with a door or window. 2. Show how to hold a fist at the end of a straight arm, with one eye closed. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Sky-watchers used their fists as a ruler for the sky. Hold your fist out like this, with one eye closed. My fist is bigger than yours. Who do you think will count more fists across that door? Why?
flow.kid: Hold your fist out on a straight arm. Close one eye. Who will count more fists across the door? Why?

good: You, because my fist is smaller.
The same, because your arm is longer too.

flow.parent: Let the reason come from your child. Many say the child will count more fists, because a child's fist is smaller. Don't correct them.

flow.do: 1. Start with your fist on one edge of the door. 2. Stack fists one on top of the other, sideways, to the other edge. 3. Count. 4. Each of you does it three times.
flow.say: Put the side of your fist on the left edge of the door. Now put your other fist next to it, then move the first one along. Count until you reach the right edge.
flow.kid: Fist on the edge. Next fist beside it. Keep going. Count the fists. Do it three times.
flow.parent: Keep the arm straight and the head still. Counts usually come out close for the child and the grown-up, because a bigger hand comes with a longer arm. But they can differ by half a fist or more. Whatever you find is a real result.

flow.do: 1. Measure each fist across the knuckles, in cm. 2. Measure from the eye to the fist with the arm held out. 3. Write both numbers in the table.
flow.say: Let's measure. How wide is your fist? How far is it from your eye? Now mine.
flow.kid: Measure your fist. Measure your arm, eye to fist. Write both numbers.
flow.parent: A grown-up's fist is often about 9 or 10 cm wide at about 60 cm from the eye. A child's might be 6 or 7 cm at about 45 cm. In both, the arm is about 6 to 7 times the fist's width, which is why the counts are often close. An adult's fist at arm's length covers about 10 degrees of sky.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think the counts came out the way they did?
flow.kid: What do you think now? What did you see? Why?

check.q: A grown-up's fist is bigger than a child's. Why can they still measure nearly the same piece of sky?
options: The grown-up holds the fist further away, on a longer arm
Fists do not really have sizes
The sky is closer to children
check.why: A fist further from the eye covers less of the view. The grown-up's longer arm puts their bigger fist further away, so it often covers about the same piece of view as a child's. If your counts were very different, this is why astronomers later built instruments with marked scales.

flow.parent: A good answer: I thought I would count more fists. We counted 5 and 4 and a half. My arm is shorter, so my small fist is closer and covers more of the view.

experiments.context: In this experiment you test the sky-watchers' fist ruler, and find out if a child's fist and a grown-up's fist measure the same.

experiments.title: The Leaking Bottle Clock: does water run out at the same speed all the way?
experiments.question: Some old water clocks let water drip out of a pot, with marks inside for the hours. Does the water level drop by the same amount every minute?
experiments.predict: Make a mark on the bottle every 30 seconds as it empties. Will the marks be the same distance apart, closer together at the bottom, or further apart? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use one bottle, one hole, and mark every 30 seconds exactly. Stand the bottle on the same flat place the whole time.

materials.item: a clear plastic bottle, 1 litre, with straight sides, label removed
a drawing pin to make the hole
a permanent marker or a strip of cello tape to write on
a bucket or the bathroom floor to catch the water
a phone stopwatch, and a ruler

experiments.safety: A grown-up makes the hole with the drawing pin. Do this in the bathroom or over a bucket, and wipe up spills.

schedule.what: Make a hole near the bottom of a bottle. Mark the water level every 30 seconds as it empties. Measure the gaps.

experiments.record: Write the gaps between marks in the table. Draw the bottle with its marks.

flow.do: 1. Push the drawing pin through the side of the bottle about 3 cm from the bottom. 2. Take the pin out and push it through again to make the hole round. 3. Put a strip of tape from top to bottom on the bottle.
flow.say: In Egypt and Babylon, water clocks let water drip out of a pot. Marks inside showed how much time had passed. Let's make one from a bottle.
flow.kid: We are making a dripping water clock. A grown-up makes a small hole near the bottom.
flow.parent: Keep the bottle cap off, or water will not flow. A hole made with a drawing pin gives a thin jet that empties a litre bottle in a few minutes.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason before filling the bottle.
flow.say: We will mark the water level every 30 seconds. Will the marks be the same distance apart? Closer together near the bottom? Or further apart? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: We mark the water every 30 seconds. Same gaps? Bigger gaps? Smaller gaps? Why?

flow.do: 1. Hold a finger over the hole and fill the bottle to the top. 2. Stand it over the bucket. 3. Take your finger away and start the stopwatch. 4. Every 30 seconds, mark the water level on the tape.
flow.say: Ready? Finger off. Start the timer. Every time I say 'mark', draw a line where the water is.
flow.kid: Take your finger off. Every 30 seconds, draw a line at the water.
flow.parent: Watch the jet. At first it shoots far. As the water gets lower, it shoots less far, and the level drops more slowly. So the marks get closer together near the bottom. If the hole clogs, poke it again with the pin.
flow.think: Why does the jet shoot less far when the bottle is nearly empty?

flow.do: Measure the gaps between the marks with a ruler. Ask your child what they think, what they saw and why.
flow.say: Let's measure the gaps. What do you notice? Why do you think the water slowed down?
flow.kid: Measure each gap. Do they get bigger or smaller? Why?

check.q: The marks got closer together near the bottom. Why?
options: Less water above the hole pushes less hard, so it flows out more slowly
The hole got smaller
Water gets tired
check.why: The weight of the water above the hole pushes the water out. When the bottle is full, it pushes hard and the jet is fast. When there is little water left, the push is smaller and the flow is slow. The Egyptian water pot found at Karnak had sloping sides, wider at the top, to make up for this.

flow.parent: A good answer: what I think, water runs out slower as the bottle empties. What I saw, the first gap was 3 cm and the last was 1 cm. Why, less water is pushing down on the hole.

experiments.context: In this experiment you make a dripping bottle clock and test whether the water drops by the same amount every 30 seconds.

activities.title: How Long Is a Minute? Test your own sense of time

materials.item: a phone stopwatch or a clock with a seconds hand
a notebook and pencil

schedule.what: Guess when one minute has passed, three times, with eyes closed. A grown-up times it.

activities.record: Write your three guesses in seconds. Circle the one closest to 60.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to sit, close their eyes and say 'now' when they think one minute has passed. 2. Start the stopwatch when you say 'go'. 3. Stop it when they say 'now'. 4. Don't tell them the time yet.
flow.say: Close your eyes. When I say go, wait until you think exactly one minute has passed. Then say now. No counting out loud. Go.
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Wait one minute. Say now when you think it is a minute.
flow.parent: Most children and grown-ups are off by 10 to 30 seconds, sometimes more. Write the time down quietly.
flow.context: This is a starting activity for the unit on how people learned to count time from the sky. You test how good your own sense of a minute is.

flow.do: 1. Try twice more: once sitting still, once while your child does something fun, such as drawing. 2. Then show all three times.
flow.say: Let's try again, twice. This time, draw something while you wait. Then I will show you all three times.
flow.kid: Try again two times. Once still, once drawing. Then look at your times.
flow.parent: Time often feels shorter when we are busy, so the drawing round is often longer than 60 seconds.

flow.do: Talk about the results.
flow.say: Were your guesses the same each time? If nobody had a clock, how could people agree on what a minute is, or when to meet?
flow.kid: Were your times the same? How could people agree on time with no clocks?

check.q: Your three guesses of a minute were all different. What does that show?
options: Our own sense of time drifts, so we need something steadier to count with
A minute is a different length each time
The stopwatch was broken
check.why: A minute is always 60 seconds. Your feeling of a minute changes with what you are doing. That is why people looked for something steadier, and found it in the sky's repeats and in water clocks.

activities.context: This short activity opens the unit. You find out how steady your own sense of time is.

activities.title: A Day of 60 Nazhigai: draw the old Indian day wheel

materials.item: a steel plate or a lid to draw round, about 20 cm across
a sheet of paper, a pencil, a ruler and crayons

schedule.what: Draw a day as a circle. Split it into 24 hours and into 60 nazhigai. Mark sunrise, noon, sunset and your bedtime.

activities.record: Keep your day wheel. Write on it how many nazhigai you sleep.

flow.do: 1. Draw round the plate. 2. Mark the top 'sunrise, 6 o'clock'. 3. Mark the bottom 'sunset, 6 o'clock'. 4. Mark noon on the right and midnight on the left.
flow.say: Old Indian astronomers counted the day from sunrise. They split the whole day and night into 60 parts, called ghatika in Sanskrit and nazhigai in Tamil. Let's draw it.
flow.kid: Draw a big circle. Sunrise at the top. Sunset at the bottom.
flow.context: This activity shows the old Indian way of splitting a day into 60 nazhigai of 24 minutes each.

flow.do: 1. Split each half of the circle into 30 equal parts, roughly, so there are 60 in all. 2. Shade every fifth mark darker.
flow.say: Each half of the circle has 30 nazhigai. 30 for the day, from sunrise to sunset, and 30 for the night.
flow.kid: Split each half into 30 parts. Make every fifth line dark.
flow.parent: It does not need to be exact. Help your child mark 5 big parts in each quarter first, then split each one into 3. That gives 15 in each quarter.

flow.do: 1. Work out together: how many nazhigai from sunrise to noon? 2. Colour your sleeping time. 3. Count how many nazhigai you sleep.
flow.say: One nazhigai is 24 minutes. Sunrise to noon is 6 hours. How many nazhigai is that? If you sleep from 9 at night to 6 in the morning, how many nazhigai do you sleep?
flow.kid: Count the parts from sunrise to noon. Colour your sleep. How many nazhigai do you sleep?

check.q: From sunrise at 6 to noon at 12 is 6 hours. How many nazhigai is that?
check.why: There are 60 nazhigai in 24 hours, so 15 nazhigai in 6 hours, a quarter of the day. Check: 15 times 24 minutes is 360 minutes, which is 6 hours. If you said 6, you counted hours, not nazhigai.

flow.parent: 9 at night to 6 in the morning is 9 hours, which is 22 and a half nazhigai.

activities.context: In this activity you draw a day as a wheel of 60 nazhigai, the old Indian unit of 24 minutes.

setup.caption: 1. Draw round a plate. Sunrise at the top.

activities.title: Count to 60 on Two Hands, perhaps the Babylonian way

materials.item: your two hands

schedule.what: Count to 12 on one hand's finger joints with the thumb. Use the other hand to count lots of 12, up to 60.

activities.record: Draw your hand and number its 12 finger joints.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the three joint sections on each finger, not counting the thumb. 2. Touch each section with the thumb of the same hand, counting 1 to 12.
flow.say: Each finger has three sections, between the joints. Four fingers have 12 sections. Touch each one with your thumb and count to 12.
flow.kid: Touch each finger section with your thumb. Count to 12.
flow.context: This activity tries one idea about why the Babylonians counted in sixties: counting finger joints.

flow.do: 1. Each time your child reaches 12, they hold up one finger on the other hand. 2. Keep going until all five fingers are up.
flow.say: When you get to 12, hold up one finger on your other hand. Start again at 1. How far can you count before the other hand is full?
flow.kid: At 12, hold up one finger on your other hand. Start again. Keep going.

check.q: Five fingers, each standing for 12. How many is that?
check.why: 5 lots of 12 is 60. That is one idea for why the Babylonians counted in sixties. Nobody knows for sure. Another idea is that 60 splits evenly into many parts.

flow.do: Talk about it.
flow.say: The Babylonians counted in sixties. Where do we still count in sixties today?
flow.kid: Where do we still count in sixties?
flow.parent: 60 seconds in a minute, 60 minutes in an hour, and 360 degrees in a circle. Historians are not sure why the Babylonians chose 60, so this is only one idea.

activities.context: This short activity tries one possible way the Babylonians counted to 60 on their hands.

setup.caption: 1. Count 12 finger sections with your thumb.

setup.art: The child's left hand holding up three fingers, and the right thumb counting again.
setup.caption: 2. Each finger on the other hand is one lot of 12.

activities.title: Eratosthenes on the Phone: compare noon shadows with someone in another city

materials.item: a pencil or a stick exactly 30 cm long, standing upright in a lump of atta dough or clay
a ruler, and a flat sunny spot on a balcony or windowsill at about 12:30
a phone call or message with a relative or friend in another city, far to the north or south, who does the same at the same time

activities.safety: Never look at the Sun. Look only at the shadow on the ground.

schedule.what: At 12:30, measure the shadow of a 30 cm stick. A relative in another city does the same at the same time. Compare.

activities.record: Write both cities and both shadow lengths. Which city is further north?

flow.do: 1. Choose a day and a time, about 12:30, with someone in a city far to the north or south of yours. 2. Each family stands a 30 cm stick upright on a flat sunny spot.
flow.say: About 2,200 years ago, Eratosthenes in Egypt found that shadows at noon are different lengths in different towns. Let's test it with Chitti in Delhi.
flow.kid: Stand the stick up straight in the sun. Someone in another city does the same.
flow.parent: This works only if your balcony or window gets sun around midday. The further apart the two cities are north to south, the bigger the difference. Chennai and Delhi, or Kochi and Lucknow, work well.
flow.context: This activity repeats the idea Eratosthenes used to measure the Earth: noon shadows have different lengths in different cities.

flow.do: 1. At the agreed time, both measure the shadow from the bottom of the stick to the tip of the shadow. 2. Share the numbers.
flow.say: Measure from the bottom of the stick to the end of the shadow. What did you get? What did they get?
flow.kid: Measure the shadow. Share your number. Whose shadow is longer?
flow.parent: In most months, the shadow in the northern city will be longer. In Chennai, around late April and again in mid-August, the noon Sun is almost straight overhead, and the shadow is very short.

flow.do: Talk about why.
flow.say: The same Sun, at the same moment. Why do you think the shadows are different lengths?
flow.kid: Same Sun. Same time. Why are the shadows different?

check.q: At the same moment, the noon shadow in Delhi is longer than in Chennai. What did Eratosthenes say this shows?
options: The Earth's ground is curved, so the Sun hits it at different slants
Delhi sticks are taller
The Sun is closer to Chennai
check.why: Because the Earth is round, the ground in Delhi is tilted a little compared with the ground in Chennai. The sunlight hits it at a bigger slant, so the shadow is longer. Eratosthenes used the difference in angle, and the distance between two towns, to work out the size of the Earth.

activities.context: In this activity, you and someone in another city measure noon shadows at the same time, as Eratosthenes did. It works if your balcony gets sun around midday.

setup.art: A 30 cm stick upright in a lump of dough on a sunny balcony floor, its shadow falling beside a ruler.
setup.caption: 1. Stand a 30 cm stick in the sun at 12:30.

setup.art: A map of India with Chennai and Delhi marked, a short shadow drawn at Chennai and a longer one at Delhi.
setup.caption: 2. Compare with someone far north or south.

activities.title: Be a Babylonian Sky-Writer: tonight's sky on a dough tablet

materials.item: a ball of atta dough, or clay, flattened into a tablet about the size of your palm
an ice-cream stick or a pencil with a flat end, to press wedge marks

activities.safety: Wash hands after handling dough. Don't eat raw dough.

schedule.what: Look at the evening sky. Record it on a dough tablet with wedge marks. Leave it to dry.

activities.record: Keep the dried tablet, and write what each mark means on a paper beside it.

flow.do: 1. Go to the window or balcony after sunset. 2. Note three things: the Moon's shape and where it is, whether it is cloudy, and any bright star or planet.
flow.say: Babylonian sky-watchers wrote down the sky every night, for hundreds of years. Tonight you are one of them. What do you see?
flow.kid: Look at the sky. What shape is the Moon? Is it cloudy? Can you see a bright star?
flow.parent: In a city you may see only the Moon and one or two bright planets or stars. That is enough. If the Moon is not up, record that too.
flow.context: In this activity, you record tonight's sky the way Babylonian astronomers did, by pressing marks into a soft tablet.

flow.do: 1. Flatten the dough. 2. Help your child make up simple wedge signs: one for the Moon, one for cloud, one for a star. 3. Press in today's date with wedge tally marks. 4. Leave the tablet on a window sill to dry for two days.
flow.say: The Babylonians pressed a reed into wet clay to make wedge-shaped marks. Make your own signs. What will be your sign for the Moon? For cloud?
flow.kid: Make your own signs. Press them into the dough. Leave it to dry.
flow.parent: The Babylonian writing is called cuneiform, which means wedge-shaped. Thousands of their sky tablets survive because baked or dried clay lasts a very long time.

activities.context: This activity turns tonight's sky into a record, like a Babylonian clay tablet.

setup.art: A child at a balcony railing looking up at a half Moon and one bright star over city buildings.
setup.caption: 1. Look at the sky. Note three things.

setup.art: A palm-sized flat dough tablet with wedge-shaped marks pressed in by an ice-cream stick.
setup.caption: 2. Press your record into the dough.

projects.title: The Window Calendar: does the Sun set in the same place every day?

materials.item: a window or balcony facing west, where you can see the Sun set behind buildings or the horizon. A window facing east works for sunrise.
small pieces of masking tape or paper stickers, and a pen
a chair or a mark on the floor, so you always stand in the same place

projects.safety: Never look straight at the Sun. Mark the place just after the Sun has gone behind the buildings, or where the glow is brightest, with a grown-up.

schedule.what: Choose a spot to stand. Mark where the Sun sets on the window glass with tape. Write the date.
Stand on the same spot. Mark the sunset place again.
Mark it again. Is it moving? Which way?
Mark it once more. Measure how far the marks have moved. Talk about how builders long ago used this.

projects.record: A row of tape marks on the window with dates, and a drawing of the skyline with the marks on it.

flow.do: 1. Choose a spot to stand, and mark it on the floor. 2. Wait until the Sun has just gone behind the buildings. Put a small piece of tape on the glass where it went down. 3. Write the date on the tape.
flow.say: Every evening the Sun sets in the west. But does it set in exactly the same place every day? Let's mark it and find out. What do you think, and why?
flow.kid: Stand on your spot. Put tape where the Sun went down. Write the date.
flow.parent: Do not let your child look at the Sun itself. Wait until it has just set, and mark where the bright glow is. Your eyes must be in the same place each time, so sit on the same chair or stand on the floor mark.
flow.context: This is the first day of the Window Calendar, a four-week project where you mark where the Sun sets.

flow.do: Each week, on the same spot, mark the new sunset place with a new piece of tape.
flow.say: Has it moved? Which way? Left or right? Is it moving towards the north or the south?
flow.kid: Mark the sunset again. Has it moved? Which way?
flow.wait: Do this once a week for four weeks.
flow.parent: Near the end of March and September, the sunset point moves quickly, by about its own width every day or two. Near late June and late December, it hardly moves for weeks. That is what solstice means: the Sun stands still, then turns back.

flow.do: After four weeks, look at the row of marks. Measure the distance between the first and last. Talk about it.
flow.say: The marks show the Sun's journey through the year. People long ago used walls, stones and temple doors to mark this, so they knew when the seasons would come. If you kept going for a whole year, what would happen?
flow.kid: Look at your marks. The Sun is moving along the skyline. What will it do in a year?

check.q: Your sunset marks move along the skyline over four weeks. What would happen if you kept marking for a whole year?
options: The marks would go to one end, turn back, go to the other end, and return to the start
The marks would keep going in one direction for ever
The marks would jump about with no pattern
check.why: The sunset point swings north until about 21 June, then back south until about 21 December, then north again. After one year it is back where it started. That swing is the solar year, and builders and farmers long ago used it as a calendar.

flow.parent: In Mexico, the Maya city of Chichen Itza has buildings lined up with the Sun on special days. In Chennai or Kochi, the sunset point moves by about 50 degrees along the skyline over the year, about five fists at arm's length.

projects.context: In this four-week project, you mark where the Sun sets on your window glass once a week, and see the Sun's yearly journey begin.

setup.art: A child on a chair by a west-facing window at dusk, pressing a piece of tape on the glass where the glow sits over a row of buildings.
setup.caption: 1. Week 1: mark the sunset place on the glass.

setup.art: The same window with five dated tape marks in a row along the skyline, spreading to one side.
setup.caption: 2. Weeks 2 to 4: mark it again. Which way does it move?

challenges.title: Make a 3-Minute Water Clock
challenges.problem: Old clock makers had to make a ghati bowl that sank in exactly one nazhigai, 24 minutes. Your challenge is smaller: make a cup clock that sinks in exactly 3 minutes, and does it three times in a row within 10 seconds.
constraints: Use one plastic cup, coins, tape, a pin and water.
You may change the hole, the number of coins, or how full the vessel is.
Test with a stopwatch, but no looking at it while the cup sinks.
materials: a drawing pin and a pen refill
a big steel vessel or bucket of water
general: Start with a small hole and widen it a little at a time, testing after each change.
Keep everything else the same, such as the coins and how you put the cup down.
Write each test's time, so you can see if you are getting closer.
creative: Put tape over part of the hole to make it a little smaller if you went too far.
Use a smaller cup, which fills sooner.
Mark a line inside the cup and time how long the water takes to reach it, instead of waiting for the cup to sink.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own clock that measures exactly 1 minute, using only things from the kitchen. Draw it, build it and test it three times.

flow.do: Read the challenge. Ask your child to plan their first try before touching anything.
flow.say: We need a cup that sinks in 3 minutes, three times in a row. What will you change if it is too slow? What if it is too fast?
flow.kid: Make a cup that sinks in 3 minutes. Too slow? Too fast? What will you change?
flow.context: This is the start of the 3-Minute Water Clock challenge. You tune a cup clock to sink in exactly 3 minutes.

flow.do: Let your child test and adjust. A grown-up makes or widens the hole each time.
flow.say: That took 4 minutes 20 seconds. Too slow or too fast? What will you change?
flow.kid: Test it. Write the time. Change one thing. Test again.
flow.parent: Changing more than one thing at once makes it hard to know what helped. Encourage one change at a time.

flow.do: Do three final rounds and check they are all within 10 seconds of 3 minutes.
flow.say: Three rounds in a row. Were they all close to 3 minutes?
flow.kid: Three last tests. Were they all near 3 minutes?

check.q: Your cup sinks in 4 minutes. You want 3 minutes. What should you change?
options: Make the hole a little bigger
Make the hole smaller
Use a bigger cup
check.why: A bigger hole lets water in faster, so the cup fills and sinks sooner. A smaller hole or a bigger cup would make it slower still.

setup.art: Three plastic cups with different-sized holes beside a steel vessel of water, and a page of test times.
setup.caption: 1. Test, change one thing, test again.

setup.art: A child pointing proudly at a stopwatch showing 3 minutes 2 seconds as a cup goes under.
setup.caption: 2. Three rounds near 3 minutes? You did it.

challenges.title: A Calendar for Planet Kuyil
challenges.problem: Kuyil is a made-up planet. It turns once a day, like Earth. Its moon goes from full to full in exactly 10 days. Kuyil goes round its sun in 73 days, and then the seasons start again. Design a calendar for the people of Kuyil, so their festivals stay in the same season every year.
constraints: Your calendar must have months that follow the moon.
Festivals must stay in the same season every year.
You must be able to explain it to a friend in one minute.
general: Count how many moon months fit in one year: 7 months is 70 days, which leaves 3 days over.
Add the 3 extra days at the end of each year as a festival week that belongs to no month.
Or add an extra month every few years, the way Indian calendars add an adhika masa.
creative: Name the months after the star groups the moon passes, like the nakshatras.
Make a calendar wheel that turns, with the 3 extra days as a special colour.
Give the people of Kuyil a 5-day week, so two weeks make one moon month.
challenges.your_turn: Now design a calendar for your own made-up planet. Choose how long its day, month and year are, and decide how to make them fit.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Work out how many 10-day months fit into 73 days.
flow.say: How many 10-day moon months fit into a 73-day year? How many days are left over?
flow.kid: Months are 10 days. The year is 73 days. How many months fit? How many days are left?
flow.context: This challenge asks you to design a calendar for a made-up planet, Kuyil, where the moon month and the year do not fit evenly.

flow.do: Let your child design their calendar on paper.
flow.say: What will you do with the 3 extra days? What happens after 10 years if you just ignore them?
flow.kid: What will you do with the extra 3 days? Draw your calendar.
flow.parent: If they ignore the 3 days, festivals slip 3 days each year, 30 days in 10 years, a whole month. This is the real problem every Moon calendar on Earth has.

flow.do: Your child explains their calendar to you in one minute.
flow.say: Explain your calendar to me in one minute. Will a festival in the first month stay in the same season?
flow.kid: Explain your calendar in one minute.

check.q: On Kuyil, 7 moon months are 70 days, and the year is 73 days. What happens if nobody adds the 3 extra days?
options: Festivals come 3 days earlier in the seasons each year
Nothing, 3 days do not matter
The moon changes to fit
check.why: Each year the moon months finish 3 days before the seasons do. After 10 years, festivals would be a whole month out of season. On Earth, 12 Moon months fall 11 days short of the year, and the same thing happens.

setup.caption: 1. Count the months in Kuyil's year.

setup.art: A paper calendar for Kuyil with month names and three extra days shaded as a festival.
