opts: The Moon going round the Earth
The Earth going round the Sun
quiz.why: One turn of the Earth gives one day and night. The Moon gives the month, and the Earth going round the Sun gives the year.

quiz.p: About how long is a solar year?
quiz.why: The Earth goes round the Sun in about 365 and a quarter days. 29 and a half days is a lunar month, and 584 days is the Venus cycle.

quiz.p: Twelve Moon months make about 354 days. What happens to a calendar that counts only Moon months?
opts: Its festivals slide about 11 days earlier through the seasons each year
It stays exactly with the seasons
It adds a day every week
quiz.why: 354 days is about 11 days short of the solar year, so a Moon-only calendar moves through the seasons. Indian calendars fix this with an extra month now and then.

quiz.p: Vani, a girl in Class 3, timed her sinking cup clock: 2 minutes 40 seconds, 2 minutes 48 seconds and 2 minutes 37 seconds. What is the best way to describe it?
opts: Nearly steady, within about 10 seconds each round
quiz.why: The times are all between 2 minutes 37 and 2 minutes 48 seconds, only 11 seconds apart. So it is nearly steady but not perfect, like every water clock.

quiz.p: Why did the ghati bowl sink?
opts: Water came in slowly through a small hole until it was full
It was too heavy to float
quiz.why: The bowl floated at first. Water came in through the tiny hole, and when it was full enough, it sank. The hole size set the time.

quiz.p: Who wrote in 499 that the Earth spins?
quiz.why: Aryabhata wrote it in his book, the Aryabhatiya. Eratosthenes measured the Earth's size, and Jai Singh II built Jantar Mantar.

quiz.p: What did the Maya track very carefully?
quiz.why: The Maya Dresden Codex has a table of Venus, which comes back every 584 days.

quiz.p: What did Chinese astronomers record in 1054?
opts: A new 'guest star', which was an exploding star
The Earth going round the Sun
quiz.why: They recorded a guest star bright enough to see by day. It was an exploding star, and its leftover cloud is the Crab Nebula.

quiz.p: Parameshvara was an astronomer in Kerala about 600 years ago. How did he find that the old eclipse tables were wrong?
opts: He watched real eclipses for many years and compared them with the tables
He read it in a Greek book
quiz.why: He recorded eclipses for decades and saw they did not come when the old Parahita tables said. In 1431 he wrote a corrected system, Drigganita. Telescopes had not been invented yet.

quiz.p: Why did astronomers check their water clocks against the Sun and stars?
opts: Water clocks drift a little, and the sky's repeats are much steadier
Water clocks only work in the daytime
quiz.why: A water clock can run fast or slow if it is bumped, if the water warms, or if the hole changes. The turning sky is much steadier, so it was used to set them right.
There are 60 nazhigai in a day and night of 24 hours, so each one is 24 minutes.

quiz.p: Karthigai Deepam is lit on a full Moon. Which star group is the Moon in that night?
quiz.why: The month Karthigai is named after Krittika. On Karthigai Deepam, the full Moon sits in Krittika.

items.p: Which repeat in the sky gives us the month?
opts: The Moon going from full to full again
The Sun coming back to the same season
items.why: The Moon goes from full to full in about 29 and a half days, and that is where the month comes from. The Earth turning once gives the day. The Sun coming back to the same season gives the year.

items.p: From one full Moon to the next takes about ____ days.
items.why: A lunar month is about 29 and a half days. That is why some Moon months have 29 days and some 30.

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: the Earth going once round the Sun
24 minutes, one sixtieth of a day
one sky body blocking the light of another
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These words come up all through the unit. The first three are the sky's three big repeats.

items.p: A calendar that counts only Moon months would keep Pongal in the middle of January every year.
items.why: False. Twelve Moon months are about 11 days shorter than a year, so a Moon-only calendar slides away from the seasons. Pongal follows the Sun, which is why it stays in mid-January.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 3, timed her sinking cup clock three times: 3 minutes 10 seconds, 3 minutes 25 seconds and 3 minutes 5 seconds. Her brother says the clock is broken. Do you agree? Explain using her numbers.
items.a: No. The times are close, all between 3 minutes 5 and 3 minutes 25 seconds, only 20 seconds apart. Small things change the time a little, such as how gently the cup is put down or water left inside. So it is a fairly steady clock, but not a perfect one.
items.why: A strong answer uses the numbers, works out the gap of 20 seconds, and gives a reason for the small differences.

items.p: Sort these festivals and days. Does each one follow the Sun, or the Moon?
items.a: see items
items.why: Festivals on the same date every year, like Pongal, Vishu and Christmas, follow the Sun. Festivals that move each year, like Deepavali, Eid and Holi, follow the Moon. A strong sorter checks whether the date moves.

items.p: Selvi, a girl in Class 4, wants her cup clock to sink faster. What should she change?
opts: Make the hole a little bigger
Put the cup in a smaller vessel
items.why: A bigger hole lets more water in each second, so the cup fills and sinks sooner. The size of the vessel does not change how fast water comes through the hole.

items.p: Put these in order, from the shortest to the longest.
items.why: A nazhigai is 24 minutes. A day is 24 hours. A lunar month is about 29 and a half days. A solar year is about 365 days.

items.p: Draw your sinking cup clock floating in the vessel. Label the hole, the coins, the water coming in, and the water in the vessel.
items.a: A cup floating in a larger vessel, with coins taped inside at the bottom, a small hole in the bottom, an arrow showing water coming up through the hole, and the water level of the vessel.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that water enters through the hole from below, and the coins sit at the bottom.
items.art: A blank box with the outline of a big vessel of water drawn in it.

items.p: Which people wrote down the sky on clay tablets, night after night, for hundreds of years?
items.why: The Babylonians, in what is now Iraq, pressed marks into wet clay. The Maya painted their books on bark paper. The Chinese wrote with brushes on silk, bamboo and paper.

items.p: The word 'ghadi', used for a clock in many Indian languages, comes from the ghati, an old Indian water clock.
items.why: True. The ghati, or ghatika, was a bowl that sank once every 24 minutes. Its name lives on in 'ghadi'.

items.p: A sundial tells the time from the Sun's shadow. Why did astronomers in India still need the ghati water clock?
items.a: A sundial needs sunlight. It does not work at night or on cloudy days. Astronomers watched the sky at night, so they needed a clock that works without the Sun, like a water clock.
items.why: A strong answer says when a sundial fails, and why night-time astronomers needed time most.

items.p: Two friends are arguing about time.

views.says: The phone gives us the real time. The sky is just pretty to look at.
The phone's time came from the sky. A day is one turn of the Earth, and hours are parts of it.

items.ask: Who do you agree with more? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing the other friend has right.
items.a: A strong answer might side with Farhan: the day, the month and the year all come from the sky, and hours and minutes were made by splitting the day. It might then grant Meena that today's phones are set by atomic clocks, which are steadier than the Earth's spin.
items.why: Both have a point. The units of time came from the sky, but today the most exact clocks are atomic clocks, not the sky.

items.p: There are ____ nazhigai in one day and night.
items.why: A day and night is 24 hours, or 1,440 minutes. 1,440 divided by 24 is 60.

items.p: Arjun, a boy in Class 3, closed his eyes and said 'now' when he thought a minute had passed. His three tries were 45, 52 and 71 seconds. What does this show?
opts: Our feeling of time is not steady, so we need a clock or the sky to count
A minute is not always 60 seconds
items.why: A minute is always 60 seconds, but our own sense of it drifts. That is why people looked for steadier ways to count time.

items.p: Eratosthenes found that at noon, a stick in Alexandria cast a short shadow, while the Sun shone straight down a well in Syene. What did this tell him?
items.why: If the Earth were flat, the Sun would make the same shadow everywhere at once. The different shadows showed the ground is curved, and the size of the difference let him work out how big the Earth is.

items.p: An eclipse pattern repeats about every 18 years. Why could the Babylonians find this pattern, when one sky-watcher on their own probably could not?
items.a: The Babylonians kept written records for hundreds of years. Later sky-watchers could read what earlier ones saw. One person sees only a few eclipses in a lifetime and might not remember them exactly. Long written records show patterns that are too slow for one person to notice.
items.why: A strong answer links the long records to slow patterns.

items.p: Match each sky-watcher to what they did.
pairs: measured the size of the Earth
corrected old eclipse tables by watching
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each one added something different: an idea, a measurement, a correction, a building and teaching.

items.p: People long ago argued about whether the Earth moves.

views.who: A follower of Ptolemy, about 1,800 years ago
views.says: The Earth stands still. If it spun, we would feel a great wind and birds would be left behind.
The Earth spins. The stars only seem to move, like the shore seems to move to a person in a boat.

views.who: Sneha, a girl in Class 4 today
views.says: I can't feel the Earth move, so I would have believed Ptolemy's follower.

items.ask: Which view do you think is best supported? Give a reason. Then say why the view you did not pick seemed sensible at the time.
items.a: A strong answer picks Aryabhata, with evidence such as photos from space or Foucault's pendulum, and the boat example. It then says that the follower of Ptolemy had a fair point, because we really do not feel any motion, and Sneha is honest about that.
items.why: This was a real argument for centuries. Not feeling motion was a reasonable objection, until people understood that the air and birds move with the Earth.

items.p: The Maya learned how to count Venus from the Babylonians.
items.why: False. The Maya lived across the ocean, in what is now Mexico and Central America, with no contact with Asia. They found the Venus cycle by watching it themselves.

items.p: Five Venus cycles of 584 days make 2,920 days. Eight years of 365 days also make 2,920 days. Why was this useful to the Maya?
opts: Every 8 years, Venus came back to the same place on the same date of their calendar
It meant Venus is 8 times bigger than Earth
items.why: Because the two counts meet at 2,920 days, the Venus pattern lines up with the year every 8 years. That made it easy to predict Venus far ahead.

items.p: Put these in time order, from the oldest to the most recent.
items: Jai Singh II builds Jantar Mantar
Aryabhata writes that the Earth spins
Chinese astronomers record a guest star
a: Aryabhata writes that the Earth spins
Chinese astronomers record a guest star
Jai Singh II builds Jantar Mantar
items.why: Eratosthenes about 240 BCE, Aryabhata 499, the guest star 1054, Drigganita 1431, and Jantar Mantar around 1730.

items.p: Rekha, a girl in Class 4, made a bottle clock with a hole near the bottom. She marked the water level every 30 seconds. The marks were 3 cm apart at the top, but only 1 cm apart near the bottom. Why? How could a clock maker fix this?
items.a: When the bottle is full, lots of water presses down on the hole and pushes water out fast. When there is little water, the push is small and it flows out slowly. A clock maker could space the hour marks closer together near the bottom, or make the pot wider at the top, as the Egyptians did.
items.why: A strong answer explains the slowing with the push of the water above, and gives a fix.

items.p: Draw a stick and its noon shadow in Chennai, and the same stick and its noon shadow in Delhi on the same day. Show which shadow is longer.
items.a: Two sticks of the same height. The Delhi shadow is longer than the Chennai shadow, because Delhi is further north and the Sun is lower in its sky at noon.
items.why: A strong drawing keeps the sticks the same height and makes the northern shadow longer.
items.art: A blank box split in two, labelled Chennai and Delhi.

items.p: Indian astronomers split the Moon's path into 27 star groups, called ____.
items.why: The Moon takes about 27 days to go round the sky past the same stars, so it spends about one day in each nakshatra.

items.p: The Tamil month Karthigai is named after Krittika, a star group. Why name a month after a star group?
opts: The full Moon in that month sits in or near that star group
Krittika can only be seen in that month
Krittika was the name of a queen
items.why: Many Indian month names come from the nakshatra where the full Moon sits in that month. Karthigai Deepam is lit on the full Moon in Krittika.

items.p: Sort these sky patterns. Could one person find each one in a few weeks of watching, or did it need records kept for many years?
items: the sunset point moving along the skyline
an eclipse pattern repeating every 18 years
Halley's Comet coming back every 76 years
the stars slowly shifting over centuries
items.a: see items
items.why: Fast repeats can be seen by one person. Slow repeats were found only because people like the Babylonians and Chinese kept written records for hundreds of years.

items.p: Riya, a girl aged 8, and her grandfather each measured the gap between two walls in fists, holding their arms straight. Both counted 5 fists, though his fist is much bigger. How can that be?
items.a: Her grandfather's arm is longer, so his bigger fist is further from his eye. Things further away cover less of the view. So his big far fist and her small near fist cover about the same part of the view.
items.why: A strong answer names both the bigger fist and the longer arm, and says why they balance.

items.p: We have 60 minutes in an hour because the Babylonians counted in sixties.
items.why: True. Babylonian astronomers used sixties, and later Greek and Arab astronomers kept them. Why the Babylonians chose 60 is still not known for sure.

items.p: Chinese astronomers wrote about a 'guest star' in the year 1054. Why do astronomers today still use this record?
opts: It tells them when the star exploded, so they know how old the Crab Nebula is
It proves the Chinese had telescopes
It shows the star is still bright
items.why: The guest star was an exploding star. Its leftover cloud is the Crab Nebula. The Chinese record gives its birth date. No telescopes existed then. The record was made by eye.

items.p: The Parahita tables were made in 683 and matched the sky well. By the 1400s, Parameshvara found eclipses coming at different times from what they said. How can tables that were good once become wrong?
items.a: The numbers in the tables had tiny errors. Each year the error added a little more. After about 700 years, the small errors had added up to a big difference. Parameshvara found it only because he watched real eclipses and compared them.
items.why: A strong answer explains that small errors add up over many years, and that only watching the sky shows the drift.

items.p: A family is talking about which calendar Indian festivals should use.

views.says: Keep the Moon and nakshatra calendar. Our festivals belong to the full Moon and the stars, as they always have.
Fix all festivals on Gregorian dates. Then schools and offices can plan holidays years ahead.
Keep both. The Moon calendar for festivals, the Gregorian one for school.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one good point from another person.
items.a: A strong answer picks one and gives a reason: for example, that the full Moon of Karthigai Deepam means something only if it falls on the full Moon, or that fixed dates help planning. It then grants a fair point from another view.
items.why: This is a real trade-off. Moon-based festivals keep their link to the sky, but their Gregorian dates move each year, which makes planning harder.

items.p: A ghati bowl sinks 5 seconds too slowly each round. It sinks 60 times in a day and night. How far off is it after a day and night?
items.why: 60 rounds times 5 seconds is 300 seconds, which is 5 minutes. A tiny error each round adds up. That is why astronomers checked their water clocks against the stars.

items.p: Design a water clock that shows each minute with a mark, so you can read the time without counting sinkings. Draw it and label the parts.
items.a: For example, a tall clear bottle filled slowly by a dripping cup above, with lines on the side marked 1, 2, 3 minutes, made by timing the rising water. Or a floating stick rising in a pot as it fills, pointing to marks.
items.why: A strong design explains how the marks were made, by timing with a clock first, and keeps the drip steady.

items.p: Your phone shows the time to the second. Where does that time come from? Is the sky still involved?
items.a: Phones get their time over the network from very exact atomic clocks. Since 1967, the second is measured with atoms, not the Earth. But the day, the month and the year still come from the sky, and leap seconds have been added to keep clocks in step with the Earth's spin.
items.why: A strong answer names atomic clocks, and says that days and years still come from the sky.

items.p: When scientists tested astrology, astrologers could match people's birth charts to their characters much better than by guessing.
items.why: False. In careful tests, such as one published in the journal Nature in 1985, astrologers did no better than chance. Astronomy, the study of where things in the sky are and how they move, makes predictions that do come true, such as eclipses.

items.p: Put these in order, from the least steady to the most steady way to keep time.
items: your own feeling of a minute
a: your own feeling of a minute
items.why: Our feeling drifts by many seconds a minute. A cup clock drifts by seconds each round. The Earth's spin changes by only thousandths of a second a day. Atomic clocks are steadier still.

items.p: The Maya and the Babylonians never met. Yet both counted a month of about 29 and a half days. What does this tell us?
items.a: They were both watching the same Moon. If two people measure the same real thing carefully, they get the same answer, even without talking to each other. This shows the Moon's cycle is a real thing in the sky, not an idea one people made up.
items.why: A strong answer says the agreement comes from measuring the same sky carefully.

items.p: Indian Hindu calendars add an extra month now and then to stay with the seasons. It is called adhika ____.
items.why: Adhika masa means 'extra month'. It is added about every two and a half to three years.

items.p: Ramzan began on about 1 March 2025. About when did it begin in 2026?
items.why: The Hijri calendar counts 12 Moon months, about 354 days, which is about 11 days shorter than the Gregorian year. So Ramzan begins about 11 days earlier each year.

items.p: Match each word we use today to where it came from.
pairs: the ghati water clock of India
the Greek word for an hour
an old word for the Moon
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Our words for time carry the history of sky-watching from many lands.

items.p: Three of these festivals follow the Moon. Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Pongal follows the Sun, so it falls in mid-January each year. Deepavali, Holi and Karthigai Deepam follow the Moon, so their dates move.

items.p: Think about this. If nothing in the universe ever repeated, no day, no heartbeat, no Moon, could anyone count time? Write what you think and why.
items.a: Any honest answer with a reason is good. For example: we could still notice that things change, such as a candle getting shorter, but without repeats it would be hard to count equal pieces of time. Or: time would still pass, but we would have no clock.
items.why: This is an open question. A strong answer gives a reason and an example.

items.p: To work out the size of the whole Earth, what did Eratosthenes need?
opts: The angle of a noon shadow in one town, and the distance to another town where there was no shadow
items.why: The difference in the Sun's angle between two towns, and the distance between them, tell you what part of the Earth's circle lies between them. From that, he worked out the whole circle.

items.p: Choose one sky-watcher from this unit. Write three questions you would ask them if you could meet them, and say why you chose them.
items.a: Any three real questions, for example to Parameshvara: How did you record the time of an eclipse? Were you ever wrong? Why did you keep watching for 55 years?
items.why: A strong answer asks questions that show what the child knows about the person's work.

open_questions.q: Why did the Babylonians count in sixties?
open_questions.why_open: We know they did, but no writing survives that says why. There are several ideas, such as 60 splitting evenly into many parts.

open_questions.q: Exactly how old is the Vedanga Jyotisha?
open_questions.why_open: Its sky positions and its language point to different dates, and scholars argue over dates from more than 3,000 years ago to about 2,400 years ago.

open_questions.q: Did Babylonian astronomy reach early India?
open_questions.why_open: Some numbers are similar, but people watching the same sky would find similar numbers anyway. There is no clear record of the journey.

open_questions.q: Were Maya and other ancient buildings lined up with the Sun on purpose?
open_questions.why_open: Some line up with sunrise or sunset on special days. For many, it is hard to know if the builders meant it, or if it is chance.

open_questions.q: How exactly were the old ghati bowls checked and made the right size?
open_questions.why_open: The books describe the bowl, but few real old bowls survive, and the details of how makers tested them are not well known.

open_questions.q: Why does the Earth's spin speed up and slow down by tiny amounts?
open_questions.why_open: Tides, the Earth's core, ice and oceans all play a part. Scientists are still working out exactly how much each one does.

maths.problem: One nazhigai is 24 minutes. Meenakshi's family watched a film that lasted 5 nazhigai. How many minutes is that? How many hours?
maths.explain: 5 lots of 24 minutes. 24 plus 24 is 48. 48 plus 48 is 96. 96 plus 24 is 120. 120 minutes is 2 hours, because each hour is 60 minutes.
maths.context: This is about the nazhigai, the old Indian unit of 24 minutes.
maths.why_maths: Changing nazhigai into minutes shows how the old Indian day fits into our hours.

maths.problem: Kavya's sinking cup took 3 minutes 10 seconds, 3 minutes 25 seconds and 3 minutes 5 seconds. What is the gap between her fastest and slowest round? Which round was the odd one out?
maths.answer: 20 seconds. Round 2 was the odd one out.
maths.explain: The fastest was 3 minutes 5 seconds, and the slowest 3 minutes 25 seconds. 25 minus 5 is 20 seconds. Rounds 1 and 3 are only 5 seconds apart, but round 2 is 15 seconds slower than round 1. So round 2 was the odd one out. Maybe the cup was put down differently.
maths.context: This is about the times from the Sinking Cup Clock experiment.
maths.why_maths: Finding the gap between times tells you how steady a clock is, and spotting the odd one out tells you what to check.

maths.problem: Venus comes back to the morning sky every 584 days. A year is 365 days. Is the Venus cycle less than one year, between one and two years, or more than two years?
maths.explain: 584 is more than 365, so it is longer than one year. Two years are 365 plus 365, which is 730 days. 584 is less than 730. So it is between one and two years, about one year and seven months.
maths.context: This is about the Maya Venus cycle of 584 days.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the Venus cycle with the year shows why the Maya needed long counts to make the two fit.

maths.problem: Ramzan began on about 1 March in 2025. A Moon calendar year is about 11 days shorter than our year. About when will Ramzan begin in 2026, and in 2027?
maths.explain: 11 days before 1 March is 18 February, because February 2026 has 28 days: 1 March minus 1 day is 28 February, minus 10 more days is 18 February. 11 days before 18 February is 7 February.
maths.context: This is about the Hijri calendar, which counts only Moon months.
maths.why_maths: Counting back on a calendar shows how a Moon-only calendar moves through the year.

maths.problem: The marks on Rekha's bottle clock were 3.2 cm, 2.8 cm, 2.3 cm and 1.9 cm apart, one every 30 seconds. About how far apart do you think the next mark will be? Why?
maths.explain: Each gap is about half a centimetre, or a little less, smaller than the one before: 3.2 to 2.8 is 0.4 less, 2.8 to 2.3 is 0.5 less, 2.3 to 1.9 is 0.4 less. So the next is about 1.9 minus 0.4 or 0.5, which is about 1.4 or 1.5 cm. The water slows down as the bottle empties.
maths.context: This is about the Leaking Bottle Clock experiment, where water slows as the bottle empties.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the pattern in the gaps lets you predict the next mark, and shows that the flow is slowing.

maths.problem: The sky turns about one fist, held at arm's length, every 40 minutes. Meenakshi saw the Moon one fist above a tower at 7:30. About what time will it be three fists above the tower?
maths.explain: From one fist to three fists is two fists more. Two lots of 40 minutes is 80 minutes, which is 1 hour 20 minutes. 7:30 plus 1 hour is 8:30, plus 20 minutes is 8:50.
maths.context: This is about telling time from how far the Moon has moved across the sky.
maths.why_maths: Adding time in equal steps turns the turning sky into a clock.

roots.context: We have built a water clock, tested how steady it is, and met the people who learned to count time from the sky. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your cup sank in nearly the same time each round, but never exactly the same. Clocks made of water, sand or springs drift a little like this. The Sun, Moon and stars repeat far more steadily. So for thousands of years, people set their clocks and calendars by the sky.
deep_truth.habit: We think time comes from the clock on the wall or the phone, and the sky just goes along with it. It is the other way round. The day, the month and the year were all counted from the sky, and the second itself was measured from the Earth's movement until 1967.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Sinking Cup Clock, three rounds with the same cup gave close but different times. Parameshvara found that even very good tables of the sky drifted over 700 years, and he corrected them by watching real eclipses.

three.who_am_i: Your body keeps rhythms too: a heartbeat, a breath, and sleep each night. They drift, like your guess of a minute.
three.what_is_life: Many plants measure how long the night is, and flower when the nights reach the right length. They keep a calendar of their own.
three.what_is_this_world: The world turns, the Moon circles and the seasons return. Every calendar on Earth is a way of counting those repeats.

roots.thread: Everything people count as time comes from a few movements in the sky. One turn of the Earth gives the day. The Moon going round gives the month. The Earth going round the Sun gives the year. From these few movements came many counts: nazhigai and hours, weeks and months, festivals, harvests and birthdays. Babylonians, Greeks, Indians, Chinese and Maya made very different calendars, and all of them count the same sky.

teachings.teaching: There is one wheel with twelve parts and three hubs. Three hundred and sixty spokes are fixed in it, and they cannot come loose. Who understands it?
teachings.link: The wheel is the year. Its twelve parts are like the months, and the 360 spokes are like the days. Old Indian sky-watchers saw the year as one turning wheel, the same repeat your Window Calendar shows.

teachings.teaching: For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven.
teachings.link: Farmers everywhere needed to know when to sow and when to harvest. Calendars from the sky told them, because the seasons come back with the Sun's year.

science.text: The day, the month and the year come from the Earth's spin, the Moon's orbit and the Earth's orbit round the Sun.
The Earth's spin is very slowly getting slower, mostly because of the Moon's pull on the oceans, so days were shorter long ago.
What time itself is, and why it seems to flow only one way, is not known.

other_view.who: Many physicists and clock makers today
other_view.view: The sky is no longer the best clock. Since 1967, the second is measured with atoms, which are far steadier than the Earth's spin. We now correct our clocks against atoms, and add leap seconds to keep them near the Earth.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if done at home with the materials listed. Choices made: the sinking cup uses a light plastic cup with two coins taped inside, because a plastic cup on its own may float even when full, and a paper cup goes soft. A steel katori was not used, because a home cannot drill a hole in steel. The hole is about 2 millimetres, the width of a pen refill tip, because a pinhole alone can take 20 minutes or more to fill a 200 ml cup. The practice round tells the parent how to adjust the hole until the cup sinks in 2 to 8 minutes, and the timed rounds allow for this. The steps say to lower the cup flat and gently, because tipping lets water over the rim. The bottle clock uses a hole near the bottom, with the cap off, over a bucket. The fist ruler is measured indoors across a door, because the sky may be cloudy or full of buildings, and its result is honestly uncertain. The Eratosthenes activity and the Window Calendar project depend on a sunny balcony or a west-facing window, so they are not in the spine. No step asks anyone to look at the Sun.

how_we_found_out.story: In Kerala, astronomers worked out eclipses with a system of tables called Parahita. It was made by Haridatta in 683. For centuries, people trusted it to say when the Moon would be eclipsed. Parameshvara was born in about 1380 in Vatasseri, a village on the Nila river in Kerala. He did not only calculate. He went out and watched. He recorded eclipses from 1393 onwards, and he wrote that he had observed the sky for 55 years. He found that the eclipses came at different times from what the Parahita tables said. The old numbers had been very good once, but small errors had added up over 700 years. So in 1431 he wrote a new system with corrected numbers. He called it Drigganita, which means 'calculation that matches what is seen'. The wrong idea was that good tables could predict the sky for ever. The sky itself showed they had drifted. Astronomers in Kerala used his system for centuries.
how_we_found_out.who: Parameshvara of Vatasseri, a Kerala astronomer (about 1380 to 1460)
how_we_found_out.when: Eclipse records from 1393. The Drigganita system was written in 1431.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought the Parahita tables, made in 683, could predict eclipses correctly for ever. Parameshvara watched real eclipses for decades and showed that the tables had drifted from the sky, so he made corrected ones.
